title: Extraocular muscles of the right eye (lateral)
attribution: 3D anatomy from Z-Anatomy, built on BodyParts3D (CC BY-SA). Rendered in Blender; surface detail added with an image model.

rows: Upper part of the common tendinous ring at the apex of the orbit.
Sclera on the top of the eyeball, a little behind the edge of the cornea.
Turns the eye upward. It also turns the eye a little inward and rotates the top of the eye toward the nose. It raises the eye best when the eye is turned outward.
Lower part of the common tendinous ring at the apex of the orbit.
Sclera on the under side of the eyeball, a little behind the edge of the cornea.
Turns the eye downward. It also turns the eye a little inward and rotates the top of the eye away from the nose. It lowers the eye best when the eye is turned outward.
hy: In a blow-out fracture of the floor of the orbit this muscle can be trapped in the break. The eye then cannot look up fully, and the patient sees double on looking up.

rows: Lateral part of the common tendinous ring at the apex of the orbit.
Sclera on the lateral side of the eyeball, a little behind the edge of the cornea.
Turns the eye outward, away from the nose (abduction).
hy: An abducens nerve lesion leaves the eye turned inward at rest and unable to turn fully outward. The patient sees double, with the two images side by side, most of all on looking toward the affected side.
Mnemonic LR6 SO4: lateral rectus by VI, superior oblique by IV, and all the other muscles that move the eye by III.

rows: Front of the floor of the orbit, on the maxilla just lateral to the opening of the nasolacrimal canal. It is the only eye muscle that arises from the front of the orbit and not from its apex.
Passes back and laterally below the inferior rectus to reach the sclera on the lower lateral part of the back half of the eyeball.
Rotates the top of the eye away from the nose and turns the eye upward and outward. It raises the eye best when the eye is turned inward.
Lesser wing of the sphenoid bone, above and in front of the optic canal.

By a wide aponeurosis into the skin of the upper eyelid and the front of the superior tarsal plate. A deep layer of smooth muscle, the superior tarsal muscle, attaches to the upper edge of the tarsal plate.
Oculomotor nerve (III), superior division. Sympathetic fibers supply the superior tarsal muscle.
hy: An oculomotor nerve lesion causes marked drooping of the eyelid (ptosis), with the eye turned down and out and often a dilated pupil. In Horner syndrome the ptosis is slight, because only the superior tarsal muscle is lost, and the pupil is small.

rows: Axons of the ganglion cells of the retina. They gather at the optic disc and leave the back of the eyeball as the optic nerve (cranial nerve II).

Runs back through the orbit inside the cone of rectus muscles and passes through the optic canal with the ophthalmic artery. It meets the nerve of the other side at the optic chiasm, where the fibers from the nasal half of each retina cross.
Sensory only: it carries vision from the retina. It is also the sensory limb of the pupillary light reflex.
hy: It is an outgrowth of the brain. Its myelin is made by oligodendrocytes, so multiple sclerosis can inflame it (optic neuritis). It is wrapped in the meninges, so raised pressure inside the skull can make the optic disc swell (papilledema).
A lesion of one optic nerve affects the vision of that eye only. Light shone into that eye constricts both pupils less than light shone into the healthy eye (relative afferent pupillary defect).

rows: The tough white outer coat of the back five sixths of the eyeball: the white of the eye. In front it is continuous with the cornea, and at the back with the sheath of the optic nerve.
Protects the eyeball, keeps its shape and gives attachment to the muscles that move it. The fibers of the optic nerve leave through a sieve-like area at the back, the lamina cribrosa.
hy: Blue sclerae are a classic sign of osteogenesis imperfecta: with too little type I collagen the sclera is thin and the dark choroid shows through. Yellowing of the whites of the eyes (scleral icterus) is often the first visible sign of jaundice.

rows: The clear, domed front one sixth of the outer coat of the eyeball, in front of the iris and pupil. It joins the sclera at the limbus.

Lets light into the eye and does most of the eye's focusing; the lens makes the fine adjustment. It has no blood vessels and is fed by the tears and the aqueous humor. It is very sensitive: its nerves come from the ophthalmic nerve (V1).
hy: Corneal reflex: touching one cornea makes both eyes blink. The ophthalmic nerve (V1) is the sensory limb and the facial nerve (VII), through orbicularis oculi, is the motor limb.
In Wilson disease copper is often deposited around the edge of the cornea, where it is seen as a brown Kayser-Fleischer ring.
